entries.title: First-order conditions of the patch optimization
entries.summary: No problem with the paper has been found; Lean has the consequences of the key inequality, but not the inequality itself.
entries.context: Proposition 4.1 shows that near any square of logarithmic size the ground state lies almost entirely in subspaces of polynomial total rank. This is what keeps the final bond dimension polynomial.
entries.claims: The proof picks density matrices xj on nested squares around the patch. Each defines a filter Lj = (xj + b·1)−aj/2, with fixed small numbers b and aj. The choice makes the norm {{tn:al-filter-norm}} as small as possible. Here Ω is the ground state. Let ρj be the reduced state, on the j-th square, of the normalized filtered state. At the minimum, each xj commutes with ρj. Also ρj ≤ xj + b·1.
entries.found: Lean proves what follows from this inequality, taken as an explicit hypothesis. One consequence concerns the operator T = bρj(xj + b·1)−1. It satisfies 0 ≤ T ≤ b·1 and T ≤ ρj. At the paper's starting radius, its trace is at most 1/4. The commutation and the inequality are not yet derived for the actual product of filters.
entries.impact: No. This is the most delicate open step, because the filters need not commute.
entries.plan: Carry out the paper's trace calculations from the largest square inward, then apply the bounds already proved.

entries.result: Lemmas 6.5–6.6, birth, death and two-sheet exchange
entries.title: Changes of owner as allowed operations
entries.summary: The lemmas hold as stated; Lean proves both with exactly the paper's hypotheses.
entries.context: The PEPS is built by handing the ground state among parties, each a label for a set of quantum registers, until every site has its own party. These lemmas are the elementary handovers, and they must use only operations that the later compression step accepts.
entries.claims: Moving a region T from one party to another is the map {{tn:peps-birth}}. Here V is an isometry that splits the buffer U around T, as in Lemma 6.4. s is a normalized state shared by the two parties. Let E be the rest of the lattice, and Ω the ground state. If I(T : E) ≤ L−60, then ‖(B − 1)Ω‖ ≤ L−30, with L the grid side. Swapping ownership of a region between two copies of the state costs at most 4L−30. Each move uses only private maps, plus normalized states or projections shared by two named parties.
entries.found: Both lemmas are proved with exactly the paper's hypotheses and error bounds. Each move acts on the actual registers, one per lattice site, each held by its owner. Adding or removing a party uses one shared normalized state or projection; the swap is a reordering that keeps every register with its party, then one private map.

entries.title: Rewriting a small patch with two-party operations
entries.summary: No problem with the paper has been found; Lean proves the lemma as stated, including the form and number of the terms.
entries.context: During the construction some small squares are stored compressed, as a short label naming a vector of a small subspace. Lemma 6.3 changes ownership near such squares, using only operations the later compression step accepts.
entries.claims: The rewrite is the map {{tn:peps-rewrite}}. K undoes or writes the encoding of a small square Q+, with tag register 𝒥. P1, …, Pm project onto low-rank subspaces of m nearby patches. M is a contraction. Its error is ‖MΩold − Ωnew‖ ≤ (m + rold)ε. Here Ωold and Ωnew are the target states before and after, rold counts changed old squares, and ε = L−60. For every a > 0, M is within L−a of a polynomial sum of terms. Each term uses private maps and normalized states or projections shared by at most two parties.
entries.found: The first part is proved with exactly the paper's hypotheses. For the second, Lean writes the map as a sum of explicit product terms, truncates each piece to rank k with error at most g/√k (g ≤ 2m, independent of the site dimensions), and reads every term as an allowed operation of Theorem 5.2 on the registers of the frames, one per site and per tag, using only parties of the specified list. With the paper's standing bound on the number of cylinder terms of each projector (one fixed power of L), boundedly many patches and affected holes, and a bounded specified list of parties, the number of terms is polynomial in L, and the choice a = 30 gives reference error at most (2b + 1)L−20. No hypotheses were added.

entries.result: Lemma 7.2, separation of the unmodified bands
entries.title: Clearance during the dyadic repainting
entries.summary: The lemma holds as stated; Lean proves it, including the paper's rule for reading ownership on boundaries.
entries.context: Ownership passes down a hierarchy of dyadic squares. Each square is repainted to its new owner by small moves along thin bands at its edges. A move is accurate only if its region stays away from other owners, since that distance keeps the shared information small.
entries.claims: There is one constant a0 > 0 such that every point y of a move's region satisfies dist(y, other owners) ≥ a0 min{n, d(y)}, where n is the side of the square and d(y) the distance from a few marked corners. Owners are read from a polygonal partition of the plane after a small generic shift off its boundaries.
entries.found: Lean builds the paper's whole schedule of partitions and proves the lemma for every square with a0 = 1/5000, assuming only n > 0. It proves that every partition in the schedule has walls on finitely many families of lines, so each generic shift gives a unique reading, and the estimates hold for it.

entries.result: Lemma 5.1, elimination of normalized pair effects
entries.title: Removing joint projections between two parties
entries.summary: The lemma holds as stated; Lean proves every clause with the paper's hypotheses.
entries.context: The compression step accepts operations built from private maps and states prepared jointly for two parties. Some moves also project two parties' registers onto a fixed vector, a postselected joint measurement. Lemma 5.1 removes these projections.
entries.claims: Each joint projection ⟨η| is replaced by a stack of m fresh shared states |η⟩⊗m. For an operation G = Σξ cξMξ whose terms have at most r projections, the replacement G′m satisfies ‖G′m − G ⊗ |Γm⟩‖ ≤ (r/√m) Σξ|cξ|, with |Γm⟩ a fixed leftover vector. The new registers belong to the original parties, and all shared states between the same two parties can be merged into one.
entries.found: Every clause is proved: the error and term counts, the locality of the new operations, ownership of the new registers, and merging any number of shared states between two parties. No hypothesis was added; the paper's assumption that the original operation is a contraction is not needed.
entries.plan: Nothing remains for this lemma. The rest of the compression argument is separate work.

entries.title: Compression needs at least one party
entries.summary: The theorem fails only with no parties, a case the paper never uses; Lean excludes it once, in a pull request awaiting merge.
entries.context: Theorem 5.2 turns the state produced by the construction, whose shared resources may be arbitrarily large, into a tensor network with one node per party and polynomial bonds. A party is a label for a set of quantum registers.
entries.claims: Let ρ be the output density matrix of the construction. For every fixed p, some such network σ satisfies ‖σ − ρ‖1 ≤ L−p, with L the size parameter. The statement does not say that there is at least one party.
entries.found: With no parties it fails. An empty tensor product has dimension one, so a construction can still multiply by a scalar c, giving density |c|2, while a network with no nodes contracts to 1. For c = 1/2 the error is |1/4 − 1| = 3/4. The paper's proof places scalars on an existing party. Lean requires at least one party once, in the definition of a construction, and repeats it on no theorem.
entries.impact: No. Every application uses an L × L grid with L ≥ 2, which has parties.

entries.title: Rectangles and triangles in a template are nondegenerate
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong with the paper; Lean reads rectangles and triangles in their ordinary sense.
entries.context: A template is a target region of the area-law argument, a union of small rectangles and triangles. The final cutting of the region into pieces whose entropies cancel uses templates.
entries.claims: A template is a finite union of the lattice points of closed rectangles and triangles of bounded size, with sides of slope 0, ∞, 1 or −1.
entries.found: Read literally, a segment or a point could count as a degenerate rectangle or triangle. The paper's remark after the definition says only the number and sizes of the pieces matter. Lean builds the ordinary meaning into the definition, so no theorem carries an extra hypothesis.
entries.impact: No. This is a reading of the paper's words.

entries.title: The low-energy sweep from its five inputs
entries.summary: No problem with the paper has been found; Lean proves the final step from five earlier results, which are not yet all proved.
entries.context: The proof sweeps a partition across a band around a target region in small random steps, while many copies of the ground state are filtered by operators built from the partition; an interpolation parameter moves the filter smoothly as a small region changes sides. Proposition 9.2 finds a point of the sweep where the filtered state has small excess energy; the later entropy bounds are applied there.
entries.claims: Some step and some interpolation parameter make the excess energy Edef = (⟨v, Hv⟩ − E0)/g small, for every large number k of copies; here v is the filtered state of the copies, H the Hamiltonian averaged over the copies, and g the gap. The proof combines the geometry of the sweep, entropy and energy transport (Proposition 7.4), norm comparisons (Proposition 8.1), entropy continuity and spectral tail bounds.
entries.found: Lean proves the step from the conclusions of those five results to the proposition; each conclusion enters as a hypothesis transcribing one displayed statement of the paper. Lean also builds the random sweep and proves its main probability bounds, but not yet all of its geometry.
entries.impact: No. The proposition holds once its inputs are proved.
entries.plan: Prove the five inputs for the actual sweep. Each is a separate item of the project.

entries.result: Lemma 8.2, routing the party network on the grid
entries.title: Routing the party network with bounded congestion
entries.summary: No problem with the paper has been found; Lean proves the lemma for every network with the four properties its proof uses.
entries.context: After compression, the approximation is a tensor network on parties attached to dyadic squares. To get a PEPS on the L × L grid, each link must run along grid edges, with each edge carrying boundedly many links.
entries.claims: The links of the network built by the construction (Proposition 7.1) can be routed with constant congestion, keeping the physical sites in place. The lemma has no hypotheses.
entries.found: The proof uses four properties. Each party sits at a point of the grid enlarged to a power-of-two side. Each dyadic square has at most B parties. Each party has at most K links. Linked parties are within c times their scale. Proposition 7.1 is not yet formalized, so Lean proves the lemma for every network with these properties. Each grid edge then carries at most 8(2c + 1)BK links. If every link has dimension at most D, the result is a PEPS on the grid. Its bond dimension is at most max(D, 1)8(2c+1)BK.
entries.impact: No. The paper's lemma is the case of its own network.
entries.plan: Formalize Proposition 7.1 and check the four properties for its network.

entries.title: Commutation of the transport operators across bands
entries.summary: The paper's hypothesis is the right one; Lean proves the proposition under exactly that hypothesis.
entries.context: The area-law proof filters many copies of the ground state, held in their symmetric subspace, by positive operators with one factor per band of a moving partition. Proposition 7.4 bounds how entropy and energy change as the partition moves.
entries.claims: The proof works with k copies of one system, whose space is 𝒱. Each band of the partition has its own positive operator. The proof assumes these operators commute on Symk𝒱, the symmetric part of the k copies.
entries.found: Commutation on all of 𝒱⊗k would be stronger. It fails when two regions overlap without nesting. Take three qubits a, b, c and k = 3. Let Wab and Wbc be the operators of the regions ab and bc. On 𝒱⊗3 their commutator has ‖[Wab, Wbc]‖2 ≈ 3.9 × 10−4. On Sym3𝒱 they reduce to Wc and Wa, which commute. Lean extends each operator by the identity off the symmetric part. It assumes exactly the paper's condition.

entries.title: The coherent measures in the transport estimate
entries.summary: Nothing is wrong with the paper; Lean builds its measures exactly as written and adds one harmless boundary case.
entries.context: Proposition 7.4 bounds how entropy and energy change as filtered copies of the ground state follow a moving partition. It writes states of k copies as averages over product states θ⊗ᵏ, through measures on the unit sphere of one copy.
entries.claims: Let 𝒱 be the space of one copy and ρ a state of k copies. The measure on unit vectors θ has density Dk Tr(ρPθ,k) with respect to the uniform measure. Here Pθ,k = |θ⊗k⟩⟨θ⊗k| and Dk = dim Symk𝒱. For each end state of the proof's averaging procedure, the measure is a Fourier-weighted average built from that state.
entries.found: Lean constructs both measures as written and proves that they are finite and reproduce the transported states. The Fourier average has total mass 1/2, as in the paper. The paper defines the end states only for interpolation parameters strictly between 0 and 1. Lean also allows an end state of zero weight, with zero measure; this is a convention, not a claim of the paper.
entries.plan: Nothing remains for this note. Using the measures on the physical data is separate work.

Spectral filtering of a finite Hermitian matrix
